elements.char: Discussion
elements.label: text

elements.char: The long-range correlated fluctuations contribute to many biological processes of the proteins,
elements.label: text

elements.char: such as allostery, catalysis, and transportation. To understand the origin of such long-range
elements.label: text

elements.char: correlations, based on the elastic network model, we conduct normal mode analysis for a large
elements.label: text

elements.char: dataset of globular proteins determined by X-ray crystallography.
elements.label: text

elements.char: First, we predict the correlated motions for proteins at different sizes. It is observed that the
elements.label: text

elements.char: correlation length of a protein can extend to the size of the whole protein, no matter how large
elements.label: text

elements.char: the protein molecule is. Moreover, with different model parameters, the scale-free correlations
elements.label: text

elements.char: and the scaling laws can be reproduced by the elastic networks model, which is the minimal
elements.label: text

elements.char: structure-based model of native proteins. Such a result indicates that the critical dynamics
elements.label: text

elements.char: characterized by the power-law relations are robustly encoded in the native topology of the
elements.label: text

elements.char: proteins.
elements.label: text

elements.char: Second, for proteins at different sizes, we conduct normal mode analysis and perform scal-
elements.label: text

elements.char: ing analysis for the slow vibration modes of the proteins. To demonstrate the particularity in
elements.label: text

elements.char: the spectrum of proteins, we compare the proteins with ideal polymer chains and lattice sys-
elements.label: text

elements.char: tems. Native proteins stand between ordered lattices and disordered polymers, acting as the
elements.label: text

elements.char: “critical point” that separates the ordered and disordered phase. Our result of scaling analysis
elements.label: text

elements.char: provides additional evidence to support the criticality hypothesis.
elements.label: text

elements.char: Third, to understand how the native topology determines the architecture and the dynam-
elements.label: text

elements.char: ics of the proteins, we conduct scaling analysis for the topological descriptors and the size of
elements.label: text

elements.char: the proteins. Our results demonstrate that, although proteins have similar average path length
elements.label: text

elements.char: with lattice structures, the residue contact networks are more modularized.
elements.label: text

elements.char: Last, we focus on the size dependence of proteins’ shape. For proteins with different chain
elements.label: text

elements.char: lengths, the most-probable shape factors always exist. Larger proteins prefer smaller shape fac-
elements.label: text

elements.char: tors. Such a constraint results from the balance between stability and functionality of proteins.
elements.label: text

elements.char: In summary, our work quantitatively demonstrates how the native contact topology defines
elements.label: text

elements.char: the long-range correlations and the slow dynamics of the native proteins. Our work not only
elements.label: text

elements.char: provides quantitative scaling relations supporting the “structure-dynamics-function” para-
elements.label: text

elements.char: digm but also reveals evolutionary constraints for proteins at different sizes. These results may
elements.label: text

elements.char: shed light on a large variety of biophysical problems such as structure prediction, multi-scale
elements.label: text

elements.char: molecular simulations, and the design of molecular machines.
